blocks.c: Chapter Twenty-Three: Recast
They poured the new Ninth in Fourthmonth, on a clear morning, at the Foundry on the north face of the ridge, and everyone came.
Sol had not understood, until she stood in that yard, how much of a bell is a decision.

She had spent three years thinking of the Ninth as a fact — a thing that was simply there, like a mast or a rib, that had always been the shape it was. But a bell is nothing except a series of choices made by people, most of them in about four seconds: how much tin; how hot; how fast the metal runs; whether the mould is dry enough or merely dry. Get any of it wrong and you have eleven hundred pounds of expensive scrap and a shed full of people not looking at each other.

Ottring explained the whole of it to Beriah Okonkwo, who was fourteen and had come up from Kettlemouth on the strength of a letter from a bell-master, and who asked so many questions that Ottring eventually made her hold the tally-board and write the answers down, which is how apprenticeships have always started.

Master Ottring was eighty-one and had refused to retire on the grounds that nobody else in the yard could be trusted with a melt. She had the old Ninth broken up and weighed and put back in the crucible, because a recast bell is a rare thing and a bell recast from its own metal is rarer, and because — she said, to a shed full of people who had come to watch — a bell that has held eight hundred tons and four hundred and eleven souls for forty-one years has earned the right to go on doing it.
Kerrin came up the Low Stair for the first time in eleven years to stand in the yard. Pel came with her and spent the whole day looking at things.
Roake stood at the front with her hand flat on the shed wall, feeling the furnace through the timber.

Dov had built something. Of course he had. It was a frame of wire and iron rods, and it stood beside the mould, and when Ottring's crew broke the plug and the metal went in with that enormous soft roar, the frame hummed, and Roake — who could not hear the pour, or the roar, or the cheer that went up from four hundred people in a foundry yard — felt every bit of it come up through the wall into her palm and she put her head back and laughed out loud.
Sol had the last of it, because Ottring made her.

"Girl. Come here. This is the alloy tray. When it's cooling you can put a thing in the crown-mould and it goes in the bell, and every foundry in the world says it's superstition and every foundry in the world does it. What are you putting in?"
Sol had thought about this for four months.

She put in a hammer-lanyard: eleven inches of spliced cord, the splice done by a woman with hands broken often enough to have opinions about the weather, cut from the lanyard Roake had been mending in the cubby at half past four in the morning on the night Sol first came to her with a story nobody would believe.
"That'll burn," said Ottring.
"I know."
"Burns to about nothing. A smudge of carbon in eleven hundred pounds of bronze. Won't change the note by a hair; won't change anything at all."
"I know," said Sol.
Ottring looked at her for a moment.
"Good," she said. "That's the correct reason. Put it in."

They hung the new Ninth in Sixthmonth. Ottring tuned it herself over nine days, taking metal off the inside of the rim with a lathe, four ounces at a time, listening after each pass with her cheek against the metal.

Sol was allowed to listen on the fourth day and the seventh and the ninth, and on the fourth day the bell was flat and sullen and sounded like an apology, and on the seventh it had begun to open, and on the ninth she put her cheek to the cold bronze and heard, in the long tail under the note, something she had been listening for without knowing it since a night on a gallery eleven months before.

It was not the old Ninth. She had half expected it to be, and had been braced to pretend. It was a different bell with the same voice — the way a daughter has her mother's laugh and none of her opinions.

On the ninth day she came out into the yard, wiped her hands, and said: "Four and one. Not four. If any hand of yours rings that bell at four flat I will come up on the ferry personally and I will not be pleasant."
"Yes, ma'am," said Sol.
"Who's ringing it in?"
There was a pause. Everyone in the yard knew what a ringing-in was, and everyone knew that it belonged, by four hundred years of custom, to the bell-master of the ship.
Tamsin Roake, who had been reading lips all morning, put her hand on Sol's shoulder and pushed her forward, hard enough to stagger her.
"Bosun—"

Roake handed her the slate. She had written it out in advance, which meant she had known for weeks, which meant she had been waiting for the day with the ordinary patience of a woman who had waited eleven years for one nod on a wharf.
Bell-master of the Meridian Gull, from the ringing-in. Papers signed and lodged at Antrell. Marn countersigned. Kerrin countersigned, which cost her a great deal and which I made her do anyway.
You will be told you are too young. You are. Everyone is. I was twenty-nine and I rang four flat for twenty-two years.

I will be aboard as ship's carpenter's mate, which is a real job and which I can do with my hands, and if you ever again put a hush plate in front of me and ask me not to use it I will throw you off this ship myself.
Sol stood in a foundry yard holding a slate and could not see any of it for about eleven seconds.
Then she wiped her face on her sleeve, because four hundred people were watching, and took the hammer.
